Vignette: Kosal

Kosal is a 76-year-old Cambodian man who has lived alone in a modest apartment for the past two decades, working part-time shifts at a warehouse on the outskirts of the city. He is quiet by nature, or perhaps quiet by necessity - it is difficult, even now, to know which came first.

He was seventeen years old when the Khmer Rouge took control of Phnom Penh. What followed were four years that he rarely speaks of in full sentences. His family - his mother, two younger sisters, and a brother - were forced from the city along with hundreds of thousands of others. They walked for days. His father, a schoolteacher, was taken from the roadside on the second morning and never seen again. Kosal watched this happen. He remembers the color of his father's shirt. He has never been able to explain why that detail stayed with him when so much else feels submerged. In the labor camps that followed, he witnessed executions, starvation, and the slow disappearance of people he had known his entire life. One of his sisters did not survive the second year. He carried this knowledge alone for a long time, not telling his mother until years later, because he did not know how.

He eventually made his way to a refugee camp in Thailand and, after several years of waiting, was resettled in the United States in the mid-1980s. He built a life the only way he knew how - through work, through routine, through keeping his hands occupied. The warehouse suits him in this way. He moves inventory, checks manifests, operates a forklift on the days his knees allow it. His coworkers describe him as dependable and largely unknowable. He brings his own lunch every day and eats alone.

Sleep has never come easily to Kosal. For decades he has woken in the early hours of the morning with his heart pounding, the images from the camp rising up before he is fully conscious - the sounds, the smells, the specific quality of light in the early morning when the guards moved between the rows of workers. He does not always remember the dreams by the time he sits up, but the feeling they leave behind lingers through the day like a bruise. He has learned to function inside this exhaustion. He does not think of it as a problem so much as a condition of his life.

Loud, sudden noises - a forklift backfiring, a pallet dropped on concrete - still make him flinch and go briefly somewhere else. He recovers quickly and says nothing, but in those seconds he is not in the warehouse. He avoids the Cambodian community events that are occasionally organized in the city. He attended one, years ago, and found that being around others who shared his history did not comfort him - it pressed on something he preferred to keep still. He has not gone back.

Kosal does not describe himself as suffering. He describes himself as old and tired, which he believes are simply the same thing at his age. He speaks about the past in a measured, distant way, as though recounting events that happened to someone he once knew. There is no anger in how he tells it - only a kind of careful flatness that feels, over time, like its own form of weight. He came to the clinic not because he sought help for what happened in Cambodia, but because his doctor referred him after he mentioned, almost in passing, that he had not slept more than four hours at a stretch in as long as he could remember.

He sits in the chair across from the therapist with his hands folded in his lap, and when asked what he hopes to get from coming here, he thinks for a long moment before answering. "Maybe just to say it," he says. "To someone who will listen."
